utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. As you can see, the Bench is complete again. Mr. Vanderpuye, unexpectedly, we see you today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Indeed, unexpectedly. Good afternoon to you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours and everyone. Mr. President, I know that you have information that Mr. McCloskey is unavailable; he's sick today. He does expect to be here tomorrow, so I just want to let you know that, in case you don't know, and so I'm his stand-in for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please forward our best wishes for his health to Mr. McCloskey. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir, Mr. Salapura. Welcome back to the courtroom. I have to remind you that the oath to tell the truth that you made at the beginning of your testimony still applies. Mr. Tolimir is continuing his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May God's peace reign in this house. May God's will be done in these proceedings, and not necessarily mine. I would like to welcome Mr. Salapura, and I would like to wish him a pleasant stay in The Hague and then a happy return home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Salapura, yesterday we spoke about the areas of responsibility because you mentioned those things in your statement, and then that was one of the elements in the book, and that element is very important for all of us. You said -- or perhaps you can tell us something about what an area of responsibility is. This can be found in document 00672, on page 13.5. This is where the zone of responsibility is regulated. My question is this: Do intelligence organs always have to know what their zone of intelligence responsibility is?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because they work within that particular zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are they responsible for what they do within the framework of that particular zone?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yesterday, you were asked whether you could go from Zagreb to Vukovar. Can you please tell us, are these two different zones of responsibility and intelligence responsibility, both military and intelligence responsibility? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely different, and I could not go from Zagreb to Vukovar. I was not allowed to do that. I was not allowed to deal with the intelligence work in that area. If I came by intelligence by chance, then I would submit that to the superior command, the superior organ, who would then know who to forward that intelligence to. They would forward the intelligence to the intelligence organ responsible for that particular area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. While we have the book in front of us, could you please tell us whether the Army of Republika Srpska was divided into the intelligence zones -- zones of responsibility, and were they subordinated to the corps commands?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the corps commands had their zones, and they were well delineated. Intelligence zone responsibility did not have to overlap strictly with the areas of responsibility of a corps. The intelligence area is somewhat wider, but that is co-ordinated by the Intelligence Administration of the Main Staff; in other words, the sector that you headed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us, when it comes to the commander of the Main Staff, is he the one who defines the areas of responsibility of the corps, and is it the Intelligence Administration who issues an order for intelligence support to define the intelligence areas of responsibility of a certain corps?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We are the ones who give such proposals to the commander, and he can either adopt our proposals or not. He can either agree or disagree. If he doesn't disagree, he corrects our proposal. And then upon his approval, this becomes a document which regulates that area. It becomes part of the decision on the intelligence support.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise to General Tolimir. I don't mean to interrupt his examination, but it's going a bit fast and I can hear that the interpreters are straining, and I'm having a little bit of trouble following, at least listening to the testimony. I would also point out, in relation to the last question, it was a compound question. The witness gave one answer to two questions, and I think if we slow down a little bit, we can probably get through this more clearly and easily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I was going to remind both speakers as well not to overlap and to pause between question and answer. It's very difficult for the interpreters to interpret everything as you tell us. Please wait after hearing the question of Mr. Tolimir, because you are using the same language, but we have to receive and the recorder has to receive everything translated into English. Mr. Tolimir, carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, and thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, please, we were not clear, obviously, and we were too fast. Let us summarise whatever we have said so far in just one question. Do the commanders of the staffs and units organise intelligence support in the areas of responsibility, and are they responsible for the intelligence support?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. For example, the intelligence organ of the Main Staff proposes the areas of intelligence responsibility for their subordinates, which are corps. The commander -- or, rather, firstly, and then the commander in our case adopts that and agrees to that, and that becomes an order for intelligence support signed by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Salapura, we're now talking about the areas of intelligence responsibility. When it comes to the armed forces of Republika Srpska, would the intelligence zone of responsibility be wider, and would it also encompass the entire international community that was involved in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our area of intelligence responsibility went in depth, and it also encompassed the territory of Croatia, the territory of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The accused's microphone is not off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it encompassed the entire territory. We also monitored the international factor on the whole in all that, because we were even exposed to air-strikes at one point in time. This meant that we had to monitor and collect intelligence about the airports from which the planes were taking off, the potential targets of the air-strikes, and so on and so forth. In other words, our territory was much wider and it went in depth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salapura. The Prosecutor introduced all intelligence from Day 1, when the VRS was established, to the last day the two of us worked, and all those documents were signed either by me or you. When I was absent, those documents were signed by you. Your organ and my organ, did we spend almost 95 per cent collecting intelligence, and that intelligence was then presented to all the end users who are mentioned in our documents' addressees?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was our job, by and large. Our intelligence was submitted daily to everybody. Our documents were not as secret as some other information that was forwarded from the Security Sector, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salapura. In the course of the examination-in-chief, you said that you were on sick leave during the events in Zepa and Srebrenica, and that you were in Banja Luka most of the time, and then you had to interrupt your sick leave because of the urgency of some developments. Since you were in Banja Luka, and since you said that I had told you that I should look after the zone in Krajina, whereas I would be in charge of the eastern part of the Republika Srpska, for the record, can you just tell us what you meant by the western part and what you meant by the eastern part? Our statement yesterday was not complete, your testimony was not complete. Could you please assist us and tell us what is it that I told you, exactly? What area were you to be in charge of, in geographical terms? Can you explain? Thank you. Thank you, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you told me that I should look after the areas of responsibility of the 1st and the 2nd Krajina Corps and the 410th Intelligence Centre, its base, and the elements within its area of responsibility and the entirety of that area, and that would go along the following line: From Brcko, that was the zone of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps, down the Una Valley towards Doboj, and then across Teslic, Mount Vlasic, up to Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the Chief of Staff Lieutenant General Milovanovic in that area of responsibility at that time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you remember whether we at that time -- bearing in mind the specific nature of the intelligence that you brought us, and that intelligence was not adequately treated, was that the reason why you were supposed to get in touch with General Milovanovic and convey all the intelligence to him directly?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I did that. I conveyed the intelligence both to the commander and him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may add to that, that when I spoke to him, I provided him with a lot more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he come under direct attack by NATO, the Croatian Army and the Muslim Army, and was there something that was contained in the intelligence that you received?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was involved in combat all the time, and the combat was going on at the time, and some of the offensives were being prepared by the Croatian Army at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown the following page, which is page 16 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And while this is being done, let me ask you this: Was the task of the Intelligence Administration and were the objectives of the overall intelligence support to collect intelligence about the strategic and tactical intelligence, and did the strategic element overtake precedence over all the other types of intelligence?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The administration and all of its organs exclusively dealt with that type of intelligence mainly of strategic importance. The corps organs dealt with intelligence of a lower level, mostly the intelligence of tactical and operative significance. When it comes to the strategic level, the international factor, all that was within the purview of the Intelligence Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber whether you, as the most capable body of our Intelligence Administration, were you in charge of all the strategic intelligence? Were you in charge of collecting strategic intelligence? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A lot of time was spent on that. Approximately 80 per cent of my time was invested in that, and approximately that quantity of intelligence originated from me, personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us whether over 80 per cent of the contents of the intelligence that we forwarded to the corps were strategic intelligence that we deemed important for the activities that the army was involved in?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not always. It's very difficult to say. In order to provide complete information, we always included intelligence that was collected by the corps intelligence. Some of the intelligence that we collected also was included if they were of some interest for the corps. We also provided some interim intelligence, not just the regular intelligence, and we forwarded that to the leadership of the Republika Srpska, the Ministry of Defence, and some other interested institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salapura. Could you please tell us whether we, in the Intelligence Administration, made sure that the corps command and the brigade commands were capable of collecting their own intelligence through reconnaissance activities and electronic reconnaissance, and we, in the administration, mostly collected strategic intelligence and data? Thank you. My question is this: Were corps capable of collecting their own intelligence that could be used for their own combat activities?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly, yes, to a certain degree. We continuously worked on that. This was a process that we were engaged in throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now look at the screen in front of us, and can you please look at line 6 from the top of the page, where it says: "Objectives of Intelligence." And I'm going to quote just one part of it: "Objective of intelligence, in tactical and strategic scale, may be geared towards planned, systematic, and co-ordinated collection of the intelligence about the enemy and the area of combat which --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this is the previous page in English. We haven't got it on the screen. Thank you. I apologise for not having said that immediately. Thank you, Aleksandar, for reminding me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I emphasised this, because I believe that this is very important. My question is this: Did you and I make sure that the command had timely intelligence based on which it could make adequate and timely decisions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we tried our utmost, and I don't think that we experienced any major surprises, and that is the goal of our work and of our existence. We would propose things, and when we look at things from this distance, we did provide quite reasonable and complete suggestions in the military and the intelligence aspect.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at page 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And while we're waiting, I'm going to put a question to you. Did you and I in the administration take into account and do our best to enable lower organs and commands to co-ordinate, in a planned manner, the operation of their organs in order to be able to compile the required data, and did we achieve any successes in that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was our co-ordinated task. We did manage, but we didn't succeed entirely. You know that we had considerable problems with our reconnaissance units. In some units, we didn't even have such units, for example, in the Drina Corps, the Herzegovina Corps, because these were units which had the greatest losses of all the units throughout the whole war. Some were destroyed in that way and were never reformed again. But for the most part, there was some things we didn't have any effects on due to the erroneous use or misuse of these units, because they were used in the most serious forms of combat, which was not actually their intent and purpose. We are not those who are commanding those units. We just control and propose, and those who use -- who decide how to use them at lower levels are the chiefs of staffs. At the level of the Main Staff, it's the commander of the Main Staff. We cannot influence and were not able to influence these decisions, and that is why I had these problems throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at the third paragraph of this page that you can see. It's this paragraph below "Centralisation." Is the principle of centralisation something that obliged lower command staffs and institutions to co-ordinate, in a planned manner, the activities of all the intelligence and reconnaissance organs and units in their area of responsibility? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and, of course, there had to be an exchange of data in order to be able to compile it or generalise the data and in order to be able to provide this data to its users at the proper time in its most useful form. That is the data that was of the highest possible interest to them at any given moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the fact that the manpower was not up to its full strength, and also the problem of the insufficient training of the cadre, for example, the command cadre and the Drina Corps came from the reserve forces and they comprised those who, before the war, did not complete the intelligence and security schools, in that case, both you and I, did we not try to organise them and, as much as possible, to help them in this organisation of the intelligence activities in their area of responsibility? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We organised seminars, we organised courses. I regularly was on the move in order to help them with any type of problem that they were facing. I wanted to help them in the way and how they could resolve these problems. They were learning as they went along. That's what the situation was like. Everybody had the same kind of situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salapura. Since we have a very important book in front of us, which is called "Intelligence Support of the Armed Forces," this is a book that is very important to us. My question is this: This rule, Intelligence Support of the Armed Forces, was that something that was the same thing and had the same weight as the Rules of Service for other organs?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These have the weight of law. They are used as the basis for activities, and they have to be respected. Any deviation from that framework would imply sanctions for action or non-action. So failure to respect these rules can imply any kind of sanction, or if they are properly applied, a person can be commended.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Salapura. Can we now look at page 21, which talks about the main assignments of intelligence support in wartime. I don't want to dwell on it too long. All I want to do is to emphasise that everything that you were asked about by Mr. McCloskey is on that page, the questions pertain to actually what your activities were. From A to P along the alphabet, all the main assignments of intelligence support in wartime are enumerated here. And perhaps the Trial Chamber can look at that so that we can look at it as well. We don't have too much time. This is like the basic manual, the Bible of intelligence work, and we can look at the first type of assignment under A: "Up to date -- timely discovery of activities and intentions of the enemy in the front area."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please explain to us exactly what that means?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that we have the obligation to uncover enemy preparations. If the enemy is preparing, we need to discover those preparations in a timely manner, which forces they plan to use, along which axis, and what the object of the action would be. Then we need to warn or inform the command organs about that of units at all levels to whom this information could be of interest. So we are obliged to discover this in a timely manner so that our units could prepare in a timely manner to respond to any possible action. This doesn't always happen. It's not always that we are successful in our assignments. There are surprises that can happen, especially when we're talking about lower-ranking levels. At higher-ranking, the strategic levels, I believe that we didn't have any surprises, I don't believe that we did. And as for the lower levels, they were insufficiently trained, and little missteps there are inevitable.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salapura.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order not to go through the whole rule, can we just look at page 24, paragraph 14, please, so that we could see what was one of the topics of the examination-in-chief yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Several times, you were asked by the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 18 in the English. Thank you, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You were asked by the Prosecutor what you ordered someone to do, what you did, and so on and so forth. Let us here look at what this paragraph 14 says about the responsibility of the intelligence organ and can it issue orders, and we're going to see that from the rules of command. Paragraph 14, here it is. It states: "The intelligence organ of the superior command/staff of the armed forces directs and co-ordinates the expert work of the intelligence and reconnaissance organs and reconnaissance units in directly subordinated commands, staffs and units, provides expert assistance, and controls their overall intelligence and reconnaissance activity." My question is this: The security organs in the administration, which was the level that we were at, did they have any other rights, other than professional overseeing and monitoring of the reconnaissance organs in the units? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, these units are subordinated from the brigade up to the corps, to the corps chief of staff. The detachment that we had at the Main Staff is directly subordinated to the commander, and all of these units were independent units. That was the status they had. A detachment -- the detachment, for example, had the status that was the same or equal to that of the brigade and the regiment, so they were subject to all the rules applying to that particular level of command and they were subordinate to the command. The intelligence organ can only, in the expert sense, propose to the commander the use of the unit, but exclusively in relation to sabotage and reconnaissance tasks. Other than that, they don't have any other powers and cannot -- and I don't think any commander would propose anything like that, because those who were in charge of those units wanted these units to be used in the manner that they were meant to be used. The use of units is something that is in the domain of the commander or the chief of staff's duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When you say that this is non-standard use, would you say that expert organs are obliged to oversee the non-standard use of some unit; for example, an artillery unit?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they are not. We are not able to monitor that either. Something that is ordered by the commander or the chief of staff, or if the unit is re-subordinated, then in that case that is not part of our jurisdiction. We only participate in the preparation of a unit, a reconnaissance unit, for reconnaissance duties, infiltration into enemy areas, gathering of information in order for an attack to be carried out in a certain area or at a military target, and we would check whether the unit has been appropriately trained for such a task in order to prevent excessive losses and to make sure that we send out the unit and that the unit comes back safely.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Salapura. Could the e-court please show page 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we are waiting to see that page, I would say this: Thus, during the examination-in-chief, reconnaissance units were referred to the most. This is 21 in English. I would kindly ask you, Mr. Salapura, to say whose are the reconnaissance units, who commands them, in whose jurisdiction they are, and what was the role of the intelligence organs in relation to these organs? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I already said that. As far as I can remember, they are at the level of the regiment and the corps, and they are subordinated to the chief of staff, as staff units. Then at the level of the Main Staff, there was a detachment. It was an independent unit, and it was subordinated directly to the chief -- the commander of the Main Staff. In the professional line, it was subordinated to the Intelligence/Security Sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salapura. Now we're going to read paragraph 21 of this Intelligence Support of the Armed Forces, which states, I quote: "Reconnaissance units of the branches and arms are specialised units of the armed forces whose purpose is to form reconnaissance organs in order to gather intelligence about the enemy and the combat area, in particular about the elements of the enemy combat/operational disposition which the units of branches and arms will engage, primarily along the main combat area in the front area, in the temporarily occupied territory and in the enemy rear." My question is this: You and I, or our organs, did we not understand each assignment in enemy territory as the most complex assignment in wartime that had to be carried out, pursuant to orders by the commander, in the sense of carrying out the assignment without sustaining too many losses or being discovered while in the field? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the assignments carried out by these units were legitimate assignments, implying legitimate targets. And in the implementation of these assignments, the main objective was to achieve the goal to make sure, number 1, that there were no civilian casualties, that there were no casualties among the UNPROFOR members at that time or members of any international organisations - this was something that was strictly emphasised in the order for execution - and to carry out the task and to return to base complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please say whether each of our assignments and every day spent on data-gathering was, de facto, work in the territory where our enemy was located and not our forces, and did this not make the life and the work of the reconnaissance and intelligence units even more difficult?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intelligence organ usually doesn't operate on its own territory. It sets off from there, but everything that is the subject of its work and interest is actually located in the territory of the enemy or the opponent. It doesn't necessarily just have to be the enemy. Looking at it from a broader perspective -- okay, we're talking only about the front here, but our work was actually much broader than that. Other than these things, we also were busy with gathering other types of information which was supposed to lead to this war ending, to communicate with certain centres in the international community that could make it possible for the war to be finished, to achieve a compromise, and to make it possible and seek out ways to actually achieve this compromise. You actually participated the most in these direct negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salapura. In order to have as little of this admitted, I would like to again just look at paragraph -- page 98, paragraph 263, and then we will finish with this document. Yesterday, during the cross-examination yesterday, you were asked about a certain order that was written to the intelligence organ. This book contains the template. I'm just going to look at paragraph 263 so that we can see what the duties are of the intelligence organs, in terms of issuing an order for any kind of intelligence task, in terms of intelligence support, that they could take responsibility for those who were going to be carrying out a certain assignment, and to be able to cover all the duties and responsibilities arising from -- any consequences that could be suffered by those who are going to carry out such assignments. So it's page 78, and it's form 3 that is attached.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We would just like the accused to point out in the English where he's reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you were asked by the interpreters to tell us from which part of this document you are reading so that can be displayed on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Please, it is item 263 in the Serbian, and we can see it also in the English. It's at the bottom of the page, whereas in Serbian it's the third from the top. I will be reading only that item. I don't want to read the entire document. We have already discussed this topic. And I will repeat for the interpreters: "The intelligence support orders (Form 3) are drafted on the basis of the intelligence support plan separately for each subordinate command, staff and units. It is drafted in commands, staffs and units in accordance with Attachment 2." And then it is listed, what it contains, but we don't have time to go into all that and read it all out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So this is my question to you: Mr. Salapura, did we have an obligation, after a commander has issued an order to reconnaissance units that were part of the Main Staff, to prepare them, train them, and to make them capable of carrying out his orders?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We would then start with detailed preparations and organisation for the mission in order to make sure that the order would be abided by. We would do that in a written form, but the units would also get a verbal order. Yesterday, a written form of order was shown here in the courtroom, something that I signed instead of the commander, but that was a document for the stage of preparation, what was necessary to be done to make sure that the unit would be prepared, from a professional point of view, for their mission, whereas the order for the mission, itself, first of all, we informed the commander that the unit is prepared, and then this order comes verbally to the commander of the unit or the commander of the group that's carrying out the assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, the Prosecutor read out to you six items from this order. I will not repeat them. Most of them referred to Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask electronic e-court to put page 104 in Serbian and the equivalent page in the English. That is page 184 or 84.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please repeat the correct page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 84, 84. Thank you. I apologise for not being clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As we can see, it's in both versions, and here is my question to you: You and I, when issuing assignments, regardless of the level of capability of commanders, and their training concerning the Geneva Conventions, did both of us insist the provision should be included in the order that would direct them to abide by the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think those could be found in the orders, and I can say that all the intelligence organs throughout the war never once experienced any situation where any of our officers failed to abide by the Geneva Conventions. This is part of our rule book, and I think it was the only rule book that included it, namely, which included the entire Geneva Conventions devoted -- parts devoted to the prisoners of war. And all intelligence officers had to take a course and then pass that course, course about the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Salapura, yesterday, during the examination-in-chief, while you were reviewing the order signed by you, you were asked the following: Why did the soldiers fire on various features there? And my question to you is: How many hand-held rocket-launchers, Zolja, did they have at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot answer that. And they weren't actually firing against features or facilities. They were firing in the air. And I don't think there were any casualties due to Zolja fire. The targets were completely different. In one of the reports we've seen, I think UNPROFOR reports, we saw that a woman got injured or killed, but we don't know what killed her. That was at 4.00 in the morning. After our team carried out its mission, and I won't go into too much detail about that, there was a lot of firing, with most of the fire coming from the Muslim side, because they didn't know what was going on. So it is possible that -- but, in any case, the mission, we carried it out professionally, competently. And I think that during the Blagojevic trial, it was evaluated as a legitimate mission. And I would like to stress again, and you know this perfectly well, Mr. Tolimir, that I was absolutely not aware of the directive in question, nor was I aware of the attack that was being in the stage of preparation, the attack against Srebrenica. And you asked me back then what my views were, and I told you that I believe that it shouldn't be done. And you said, I think the same. And that's when we said goodbye to each other. You stayed in your office, and I went for sick leave. But I was not aware that we were preparing anything of the kind, nor that there was any directive drafted in March, because I did not take part in any planning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salapura. The document that the OTP showed to you today was a summary of events drafted by UNPROFOR, which was based on comments by witnesses, Muslims. And in this document, there was no mention of any facilities or buildings being damaged, which demonstrates that the rocket-launchers were fired up in the air, because if it were not so, the 15 or 16 rockets would have hit the buildings, which they didn't, based on this document by UNPROFOR which showed how the events took place. My second question to you is: Is it possible that this woman got killed through the activity or your team, because as far as I remember, we didn't have any information about any casualties on their part or on ours?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, please wait that the interpreters can catch the whole question of Mr. Tolimir. Otherwise, we will lose some of your answers. Please repeat your answer now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we did not have such information, nor did we have any information -- did we receive any information later on in our contacts with the Commission for Negotiations with UNPROFOR in Vlasenica, because the purpose of this mission was to warn the other side and to alert UNPROFOR to enemy activity on our side, and we had even reports by the 28th Division about their activities. They sent it to their command at Tuzla, but we also had our reports which we were forwarding to UNPROFOR all the time; namely, that we have constant losses and casualties after activities that had been launched from the so-called demilitarised area. But it wasn't a demilitarised area. They were still being armed. And we knew, also, when they were bringing it in. We even managed to shoot down a helicopter that was bringing in weapons into the Srebrenica area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm on my feet really because the question that was put to the witness, which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In fact, there were two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The question that I'm focusing on was, I think, at page 23, line 11 -- or page 22, rather, line 11, and the question was pretty simple, which was whether or not it was possible that this woman was killed as a result of the activities of the witness's unit. He's gone on now for it looks like the better part of 10 or 12 lines. He hasn't answered that question at all. And I think it would be more efficient if the witness could answer the questions that are put by General Tolimir to the proceedings, and I think it will make the record more clear, and I think the matter -- I think it's a better way forward than this. He's done it on a number of occasion, and that's the reason why I'm on my feet now, because I think it would just be a better way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The best is always just to put one question at a time and not a compound question or several questions at the same time. I would like to repeat the question of Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Salapura. I repeat: "Is it possible that this woman got killed through the activity of your team, because, as far as I remember, we didn't have any information about any casualties on their part or on ours?" That was the question. Could you please answer this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we did not have any information about any casualties on the Muslim side. It is possible, though, but it's very difficult to say that with any certainty and to determine whether this woman got killed due to our fire or as a victim of Muslim fire in return. We don't even know where did she get killed. Was it out there in the street, in a building? It was 4.00 in the morning. And also, if it was our fault, well, it's wartime, it was part of a combat activity. It is possible that some of our soldiers failed to abide by the orders, failed to shoot up in the air. It was night-time. It is possible. I cannot say, with any degree of certainty, no, it wasn't, yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. But hearing this answer at line 13, page 24, the witness is -- it's recorded in the transcript that he says that this was part of a combat activity. And I believe his prior testimony, at least up until this point, was this was a sabotage operation, and I'm not clear, from the record or from his testimony, whether or not this is an accurate transcription of what he says or interpretation of what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I think you, respectively Mr. McCloskey, should deal with that in re-examination. We have to rely on the interpretation. Mr. Tolimir may put this question to that part again or carry on. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. McCloskey, on page 80 of the transcript, yesterday's transcript - I don't know whether this page still bears the same number - he said: "You heard Karadzic say that Srebrenica needs to be terrorised. Wasn't that the reason why it should be terrorised?" And he was discussing -- he was referring to this sabotage mission in Srebrenica. And you, on page 81, line 7, said: "No, the projectiles were fired in the air. I was against the use of weapons ..." And so on and so forth. Again, Mr. Vanderpuye is now asking you -- well, you've heard his question, but this is my question to you: Sabotage units, are they a part of a unit that can be used for any type of activity, including demonstration of power and so on? Were they carrying out actions, and did they receive orders?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sabotage actions are combat activities, just like any other combat activity, so they are only carried out behind the enemy lines, and they are carried out by special units that are called sabotage or reconnaissance units or just reconnaissance units. Maybe it would be good if I explained that. They are something like special units. Like in Pakistan, the killing of bin Laden was most probably carried out by one such unit. These are units that are trained specifically for missions behind enemy lines. Regular soldiers from regular units would not normally go five, ten, fifteen, twenty kilometres behind the enemy lines. That's not what they are supposed to do. I hope I've been of assistance. These are combat activities. The front-line units are carrying out combat activities along the front-line, and these units are carrying out their combat activities behind enemy lines, but all of them have certain objectives and it's just one of the aspects of combat activities, attacking activities. I hope I've managed to help you understand this better.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Salapura. We will later show a document where we can see that Muslims are reporting they have had no casualties. I will show that to the Trial Chamber after the break. I would like to tender this Intelligence Support for Armed Forces, which includes the Geneva Conventions. So can we please have this tendered?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, if I'm not mistaken, you indicated you would tender the relevant parts you have used with the witness, and not the whole document, which is really a lengthy document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I don't mind. However, the Prosecutor always objects if we tender just one part because they believe that we only use the part that suits us. If the Prosecutor doesn't object, the document has been translated, all of it, so whatever you decide, I will abide by your decision. And it is on the Prosecutor's 65 ter list, the whole document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't see any objection by the Prosecution, and I don't recall similar instances. It is only a question of practicability. If you have such a big document in evidence, you have to deal with that later on as well, like the Chamber and the Prosecutor. It was only the question you indicated earlier today that you will only tender those parts you have used with the witness, and I would like to invite you to point out which pages you want to have in evidence. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We don't have an objection to the admission of the entire document, if that's what General Tolimir wants to do. I understand that it is burdensome to the record and it is a lot of material, but I think, as the proceedings continue, there will be other parts of this document and also, indeed, other documents that will be referred to. So it might as well serve all of our interests to have the document admitted in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, again, are you tendering the whole document or only several parts?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to tender the entire document, because I can see that the Prosecutor wishes to do the same. I don't want the Prosecutor to say that I am tendering only that suits me. I want to avoid any objections of that kind on the part of the Prosecutor. Therefore, I would like to tender the entire document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document 65 ter 372 will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D229, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly to show D202, item 6 or Article 6 on page 2. And while this is being done, I would like to say that this is a book of regulations on the competences of the corps commands in peacetime. Thank you. I'm interested in Article 6 on page 2 in Serbian and on page 4 in the English version, the corresponding Article 6. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can now see the first paragraph that you have quoted from on a number of occasions. You were a commander, so you know it. I'm quoting from the beginning of Article 6: "The right to command units and institutions of the organic compound of Land Army Corps is under the exclusive responsibility of the commander." Thank you. Why am I quoting this? I am quoting this because on several occasions yesterday, you were asked whether the Command of the Drina Corps was abreast of the activities in the tunnel, about the sabotage activities in the tunnel or through the tunnel. That was on page 58, 19, of yesterday's transcript. On several occasions, you were asked, although you had already said on page 58, 19, that it was the Drina Corps Command that requested that, so I would like you to say that for the record clearly, and then I'm going to quote from something else. I'm going to quote from page 60, and this was on page 58. And later on, I'm going to quote from page 60, where a question was put to you whether the detachment was used in a proper manner, whether the command had been informed about that. Could you please tell us now whether Krstic was abreast of the situation, and whether the activities in the tunnel and the use of the Sabotage Detachment had been requested by the corps command, and whether the request had ever been forwarded to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please wait with your answer. Now, continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The action was carried out upon the request of the Command of the Drina Corps. The commander of the Main Staff approved the activity and issued his own order for me to look at the overall situation and to see whether that operation was feasible, what were the levels of risk, whether the desired effects could be achieved, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Salapura. Let's look at page 60 now, all of us together. That's in the transcript, page 60. That's part of your cross-examination, and you say: "The Drina Corps chief of staff, Krstic, received from the commander of the Main Staff approval to engage the sabotage unit in the tunnel. I know that the commander, himself, gave it to me personally. Tolimir was not there ..." And so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, my question is this: When it comes to all of those activities tied with the tunnel and the engagement of the sabotage unit in the tunnel, were they approved by the commander of the Drina Corps and the commander of the Main Staff? Had they been planned in their plans of activities?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. A clear order was issued, as you could see. I signed it myself. The order was for the engagement of the detachment, and it specified what else had to be collected. And an order was issued to avoid any casualties among the civilian population and among UNPROFOR soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salapura. Likewise, during the examination-in-chief about what Mr. McCloskey called as terrorising our organs, who didn't know anything about that, as you said, on page 35 of the court transcript, Mr. McCloskey started talking about a document before he showed it and tendered it subsequently, and then he said, I can quote. I would like to call up P124, where he says in the Cyrillic version, on the 8th of March, 1995, Radovan Karadzic, the text was drafted by General Radovan Miletic and it was signed by Spasoje Zeljkovic, or rather, he typed it. And then he asked you whether you knew Miletic and Zeljkovic. Later on, on page 39 of the record, you were asked several questions about your knowledge of Miletic's participation in this document. My question is this: Did you personally -- from Prosecutor on page 35, four pages before 39, that he had learned, through the document, who signed it and who had drafted it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know who drafted it. I didn't know who typed it before it was shown to me. I saw the initials on the document, but I didn't see them before, before the Prosecutor showed the document to me. I repeat that I was not informed by that, nor did I participate in any shape or form in the drafting of that document. I didn't even know about its existence. I only learnt about its existence after the war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you are referring to different pages. I take it that you are referring to the transcript of yesterday's hearing, just for the clarity of the record. You mentioned cross-examination on page 60 of yesterday's transcript. That was not cross-examination. That was, indeed, examination-in-chief, just to make it clear. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for your very correct corrections. I apologise for making mistakes. It happens often. I get confused when it comes to cross-examination versus examination-in-chief. I have another question for Colonel Salapura here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That part referred to by Mr. McCloskey, was that written in the facility -- or, rather, in the document prepared by the security organs or was it part of something that is drafted by other organs? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. What are you referring to? What are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think it would be helpful to have P124 up on the screen. Then you can put a question to this document. It is very difficult for the witness to follow your kind of questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We are heading towards the break. I can repeat the question, and then if it's not clear again, then I will repeat it. The document is P1214. We will see it later to jog the witness's memory. Mr. McCloskey was quoting from the directive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I want to know the correct number. First, you said "124," and now you say "P1214." Which is the correct number? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is P1214.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We should have that on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. While we are waiting for that - we are very restricted on time - could you please answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey spoke to you about some terror. When it comes to that part of the proposal dealing with the enemy elements, where it says -- did you inflict terror on the entire inhabitants of Srebrenica when you sent your sabotage unit there? Can you answer?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, that operation, in my mind, and I was the one who gave an order for its preparation, and I had informed the commander that it could be carried out, that it was feasible, it was, indeed, carried out. As far as I'm concerned, that operation had nothing whatsoever to do with any directives or with what Mr. McCloskey said yesterday, and that was that General Karadzic wrote in that directive that life should be made unbearable for the Muslim population. Let me repeat, I didn't know anything about that directive. That directive had nothing whatsoever to do with our operation, or, rather, the operation did not constitute any infliction of terror. It was just a classical form of a sabotage operation which was carried out very carefully, very fairly. It was a very professional operation. It was a textbook example of a professional military operation behind the enemy lines. The weather conditions were very bad. Still, the operation was carried out very correctly, without any casualties. Yesterday, Mr. McCloskey told me that one woman got killed. Well, it was war. I'm not denying that fact. However, I cannot claim that the casualty was the result of our fire. Mr. McCloskey also knows that there was a report from the Muslim side about no casualties, and we received the same report from UNPROFOR, and that would be that. And that had nothing to do with any infliction of terror. It was a classical professional, superbly carried out and legitimate operation that was carried out by a unit of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. I am very proud of it, and I can claim there were no casualties as a result of that operation. We suffered casualties on our side, but that's neither here nor there. There was casualties before the operation and after it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salapura. And while we have the document on the screen, my question is this: Was it up to the intelligence organ to formulate all the tasks for the VRS and the corps? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was the commanders who were tasked with that. It was not up to us to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are we looking at the first chapter entitled "Main Characteristics of the International Military and Political Situation," and did we participate in the drafting of this paragraph together with the other organs of the command who had information about the military and political situation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intelligence organ does provide the input for paragraph 1, about the enemy army and the international factors, but it is not just the intelligence organ. It could be done together with the organ for morale, religious and legal affairs. We could do it jointly in order to define that political part of the directive.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Salapura. We no longer need this document which we see on the screen, but we don't need it anymore. Can we now see 1D743 instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is your statement that you provided in Banja Luka on the 21st of July, 2004, when you were interviewed by the investigators of this Tribunal. Thank you. Can we please look at page 14 first, lines from 7 through 13. That's page 13 in English. And I also have to give you a reference because of what I asked you about the areas of responsibility, and here, in lines 7 through 14, you spoke about the areas of responsibility of the corps. That's why I'm giving you this reference. My question is this: Since the security organs give proposals to the commander, what would be the zones of intelligence security, do they have any right to issue orders with respect to anything to the commands of corps and brigades in these areas of responsibility, with the prior consent of their commanders?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they don't have that right. And I, as the chief of the Intelligence Administration of the Main Staff, did not have the right to issue any organs [as interpreted] to the intelligence organ in the corps. In other words, I can provide intelligence. That was my obligation. His obligation was to provide me with intelligence. If there is something of special interest to me, then I have to draft a document entitled "A Request for Intelligence," and I address it to the chief of staff to whom that intelligence officer is subordinated, the intelligence organ of the corps. And then I can ask him to collect certain intelligence for the Main Staff and to submit that intelligence to me. I have to do it through the chief of staff, and it is the chief of staff who decides who will collect that information or intelligence. In other words, we don't have any authorities in terms of command responsibility over the intelligence organs at the lower level, and we don't have that same authority over lower units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, while we're discussing this issue, could you please tell us, who has the exclusive power of command over troops of the corps and their subordinated units, according to the rules governing powers of the corps of the land army?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exclusively, the commander and, for the staff units, the chief of staff. So there are only two persons who have that power.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have D202, or, rather, not D202, but D148, items 115 and 116. Thank you. D148, items 115 and 116.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you have used 1D743, the OTP statement of the witness. Will you use it again or what will you do with it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll use it again. I just would like to illustrate the last answer provided by the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have it in the e-court. And here we have the rule book on corps. We can see item 115, where the brigade commander is discussed, and item 116, which discusses the staff. I will just read the first sentence: "The brigade commander has the exclusive right to command all brigade units and attached units." The last line is as follows: "The commander takes decisions, assigns tasks to units, monitors their fulfillment, and demands their strict execution, regardless of difficulties that arise."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And this is my question to you: Is this a good reflection of your comments in answer to my question about the powers of command?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we were a specific structure, the intelligence organs of lower levels were commanded by chiefs of staff and commanders of units, so let's see what does it say about the staffs. It says, under 116: "The staff is the main organ of the brigade command, and it functionally links and integrates the operations of all command organs. "The chief of staff directs the work of the staff. He is also the deputy commander of the brigade. The chief of staff, in accordance with the commander's decision, has the right to assign tasks to subordinates." And so on and so forth. So this is my question to you: In addition to having the right to command the subordinate units, upon being authorised by his commander, did he also have the right to command the intelligence organs at lower levels? Was that part of his powers, for instance, from corps to brigade?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Intelligence organs in the corps and the brigades were subordinated to the chief of staff, and they were part of the staff. The reconnaissance units within a brigade, or also the reconnaissance sabotage unit within the brigade, was subordinated to the chief of staff. It was different only at the level of the Main Staff, because we had a sector there and the organisation was completely different. The Sabotage and Reconnaissance Detachment of the Main Staff was subordinated directly to the commander, instead of to the chief of staff. Because of the existence of the sector, the intelligence organ which I headed was not subordinated to the chief of staff, but to the sector, and then the commander via the sector, and that was the specific situation with the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Salapura. We will not embark on the next set of questions because it's time for the break. We will continue after the break. Thank you, Mr. President. If it's okay with you, I think we could go for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, it is time for the first break, and we will resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You need your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise. Before we move to another topic, I would like e-court to show document 1D752, please. This is a statement by a Muslim about this event in the tunnel. I remember seeing it. We didn't want to up-load it immediately into e-court, not to burden the case with too many documents, but now since there's a need, we have issued instructions that it be up-loaded. Thank you. We can see it on the screen. Could you please zoom in a little bit. I would like to state for the transcript that this document is a document by the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the 28th Division Command, of the 27th of June, referring to the events in the tunnel, and it was signed personally by the stand-in for the commander, Chief of Staff Major Ramiz Becirovic, who was acting for the commander because the commander was away. And I am quoting from the document: "I received your letter of the 26th of June, 1995. I am glad that you are all fine and healthy. The complete situation in our encirclement is something that you're familiar with in detail. So far, we are successfully coping with all the problems. The aggressor's action in the depth really did surprise us, but it is a piece of luck that it all ended the way it did. We took certain steps, and we will do everything required in order to prevent this or something similar from happening again. Activities are underway to seal the pit," talking about the mine pit. "Engineers of Rudnik have been engaged, and promise has also been helped by representatives of the UN forces. I am constantly making efforts to camouflage the army in relation to the representatives of the UN." Right, so he's talking about how they're concealing the military activities in this zone: "And I can tell you that there are some incorrect things on their side."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, please, does this report by Ramiz Becirovic, that is being sent to Tuzla, to the commander of the 2nd Corps, on the 27th of June, does that refer to these events in the tunnel? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, please, is there any information in this report about the losses and about the death or killing of a woman in this action, or is it just talking about the surprise element?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we can see here that there is no such data there, and it says that it was a piece of real luck that that's how it turned out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could I tender this document, 1D752, into the evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D230, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at 1D743, 1D743. This is the witness's statement. He referred to the statement also during the examination-in-chief by the Prosecutor during the first two days of his testimony. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see your statement here that we partially already attempted to utilise, so, please, during your examination -- actually, the cross-examination, and during the resume, on page 6 -- on page 4 of the 2nd of May, the Prosecutor briefly referred to your CV. So on page 4, lines 9 -- on line 5.7, you said what you did, and at one point you said that you happened to be in Zagreb when the war broke out in 1981 and 1982 [as interpreted], that you completed your education, and so on and so forth. Can you please tell us: During the war, were you in Croatia in the 5th Military District Command in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether the District Military Command had any losses, and what were these loss, and what was the conflict? What can you tell the Trial Chamber about this conflict that was taking place in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in the command building? We did have casualties. Is that what you're referring to? Two people, two men. They were attacking. We were inside. In the evening, we were attacked by the ZNG. This would begin at nightfall and then last all night until dawn. Observers were there, international observers, only in day-time, and I think one of the European observers was injured, wounded, when he was in the building where we were. And this went on for about a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: For the transcript, could you please tell us what the ZNG is? Who is that? Who did that armed formation belong to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the Croatian National Guards, and they belonged to the Croatian forces. That was the name of the Croatian Army in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And the Croatian National Guard, according to the rules at the time, were they a paramilitary unit and did they present themselves as a legitimate military force in relation to the JNA in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, that military force was not recognised as a legitimate military force, and Croatia was not recognised either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, from the transcript, when were you transferred to Slunj from Zagreb, and then when were you transferred from Slunj to Sarajevo? And I'm talking about the Command of the 5th Military District. This is something you talked about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, but it's a bit difficult --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you again. It is very difficult. Again, you are overlapping, you are too fast. Please pause between question, answer, and the next question. Now your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It would be hard for me to give you the exact time and date. I am having some problems with numbers. I've already mentioned that. I have memory problems mostly in terms of numbers, so it's hard for me now to say exactly when this was. 1991, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salapura. Could you please answer this question: Was this -- these events in Croatia, when you had to leave Zagreb as the legal army and the military district command, and when you went to Slunj and then from Slunj to Sarajevo, did this occur before the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, before the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, before the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, before the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you happen to remember who was the supreme commander to me, as well as to you, to all of those who were defending themselves and those who were attacking?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Stipo Mesic -- Stipe Mesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, for the transcript, where was Stipe Mesic from, from which state, Stipe Mesic, who was our commander-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us whether it's a precedent that the supreme commander happens to be from the republic that was trying to secede legitimately, that he was trying to drive the legitimate military forces out of the republic of Croatia, and how appropriate was it that he was the commander to both me and you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, sir, sir, again, just now the translation has stopped. It is impossible to catch everything if you are both really speaking at the same time. I had to stop you again. Please look at the transcript, and then you will see when the record stops. Then you should start with your answer. Please bear that in mind. And now your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in essence, that's exactly how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since we were interrupted, and you have to say for the transcript, what is it that it was, the way it was, could you please give us an entire sentence, the subject, the object, and all the other relevant parts of the sentence, so that we know exactly what we are talking about here? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Mesic, as the supreme commander, right from the beginning, from the time he took up this duty, worked on the break-up of Yugoslavia, and he gave a public statement that he was the bankruptcy president, that he was going to dismantle the state as it was. So this is what he was working on, and this is what actually happened, along with the support from Tudjman and a number of European countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you this: Since you were working on gathering data, did you have information as to whether the European Union and others who participated in the achievement of a peaceful solution exerted pressure on Yugoslavia that Stipe Mesic be elected president of the Presidency for that particular period of the presidential term of office?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't give you a firm answer to that question, because in that time-period, I was not really carrying out these type of duties. I know -- well, all right, it doesn't matter who was elected. Actually, I really am not able to give you a specific answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salapura. And now, please, do you remember the statement that Stipe Mesic gave after the war between Croatia and Yugoslavia ended, Croatia seceded, after it was recognised, and after he left the post of supreme commander because he could no longer be the supreme commander because he was representing a country that had seceded from the main body of the country?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say exactly, I couldn't quote to you the statement that he gave. But later, when he was still at that post, I attended negotiations in Pakrac, where he also was present. And, no, I know that he was satisfied that the process was proceeding in that way, the process of breaking up of Yugoslavia. He stated that openly at the time, stating that these were the goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Salapura, do you remember if at the time, 1991, until the war in Yugoslavia, were there any Muslim officers in Bosnia and Herzegovina who later took up posts in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? These were commanders like Delic, Dudakovic, Hadzihasanovic, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in Croatia before the war. They were part of the then legitimate army of Yugoslavia, the JNA. Then they -- with the transfer of the 5th Corps units to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, they also were transferred, and then they stayed in units that were stationed in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, until the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised. I don't remember the dates when they were individually leaving. I think Enver Hadzihasanovic was the last one to leave. He was the commander of the 49th Mechanised Brigade in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Salapura, as you were in Sarajevo, can you please tell us, while the war was underway in Croatia, the UN observers and other peace observers, were they located in Sarajevo, and did not the federal state provide them with a fleet of vehicles that they could use?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These were representatives of the international community, and then this military mission arrived from Zagreb. It wasn't a large mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to tell us, were you following that? How come that Bosnia and Herzegovina was an oasis of peace for representatives of international community who were intermediating or mediating in the international conflict until the war broke out in Croatia, and then they transferred all of their people to Croatia, after which the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina? How could this happen? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I've understood your question fully. But upon our arrival in Bosnia, there weren't that many peace forces present in Bosnia, international peace forces. There were exclusively observers present, and only later the military segment joined. I think it was with the arrival of Satish Nambiar and some other officer, General MacKenzie as well. Together with them, a larger group of military people arrived to Bihac, Sarajevo, Tuzla, and some other locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, do you remember where the staff of Mr. Akashi was located?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in Zagreb, yes. Yasushi Akashi had his headquarters in Zagreb. That was their headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The headquarters, Mr. Yasushi Akashi's headquarters, was it there in Zagreb, in Croatia, during the war in Croatia as well, or was it only that it was established after the war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the war in Croatia ended. They were there during the war, but they were called European Union observers. And after the war in Croatia ended, the UN had its headquarters located in Zagreb. That was the initial stages of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salapura. That was the gist of my question, namely, Mr. Akashi and the United Nations, and I do remember you telling us about observers being there before them. Thank you. Could you please tell us whether, in Yugoslavia, all republics were recognised -- or, rather, that all the states that seceded from the former Yugoslavia were recognised, except for Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first state or republic that seceded was Slovenia, and it was a relatively peaceful process. The next one was Croatia, and after that, and I believe it was something that international experts would agree with me, it was Bosnia and Herzegovina which seceded according to a very urgent procedure. And then later on, it was Macedonia, and then relatively recently, Montenegro as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
