utterances.text: Thank you. You first said that Slovenia seceded. Were there any troops of the 5th Military District deployed in Slovenia, and did they have any casualties?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there weren't many casualties because the attack was launched against the JNA units, but the conflicts didn't last very long and there were not that many casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were part of the institutions that were charged with protecting the constitutional order, could you please tell us whether all the republics of the former Yugoslavia were recognised by the European Union before Serbia got its international recognition?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were all recognised rather quickly, rather quickly, very quickly. It was according to some kind of urgent procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let us look at page 6 of your statement, lines 3 to 7.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the statement on the screen, 1D743. Thank you. Thank you, Aleksandar. Page 6 in B/C/S, page 5 in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In line 3, you're saying: "Well, after the Dobrovoljacka Street massacre in Sarajevo --" The interpreter says: "Dobrovoljacka?" And then you say: "Yes, Dobrovoljacka. I was in that column, in that convoy. Those who were there in the column know about it. Yes, I ended up in the Military Hospital in Sarajevo, and about 15 days later I arrived in Han Pijesak ..." And so on. Now, this is my question to you: Could you please tell us, for the record, where exactly is this Dobrovoljacka Street, and when did this massacre take place in Dobrovoljacka Street in Sarajevo? What was that convoy that is being mentioned here, who attacked it and who was the victim? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dobrovoljacka Street is a street in Sarajevo on the left bank of the Miljacka River. I think that part of town is called Mejtas. I think so. I'm almost certain. The attack was launched against a part of the Command of the 5th Military District, together with the commander, who remained in the area for the purpose of negotiations with the leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or, rather, the Muslim/Croatian leadership, because the Serbian representatives in the leadership withdrew from all BH institutions and went to Pale. The negotiations went on for days, I don't know how many days exactly, and then suddenly we were being exposed to attacks usually during the night, but occasionally during the day. This went on for about 10 days. They switched off our electricity supply, water supply, communications with our command. And during the day, negotiations were going on with international intermediaries being present. And towards the end, the president of the rump Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic, late Alija Izetbegovic, came to Dobrovoljacka Street, and he and General MacKenzie provided guarantees, saying that the command can have safe passage to Lukavica, where the barracks were. We soon discovered that there were ambushes set up along our route. And in the office of the commander, we had discussions, while I was also receiving information from our operatives about MUP and Green Berets. I was warning the commander that regardless of the guarantees, there will be an attack. We then received another set of guarantees. But as soon as we set off in a convoy, we were attacked from both sides of the street. There was video footage of that. It was in early May. I'm not sure exactly what date it was, but it was early May. We had lots of casualties. There were dead and wounded. There is, I think, a proceeding going on about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, just a moment, please. I'm not sure if we have really the -- if the translation reflects exactly what we have in English on the screen. If you compare the subsequent passages and paragraphs, I think that there is some difference. I'm not sure about the accuracy of this translation. I just want to put it on the screen -- on the record so that we have to check it at a later stage. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, do you know which event started the First World War?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was one cause, and there was a different thing that started it. It was an assassination of Franz Ferdinand, the Austrian emperor, that was carried out by Gavrilo Princip in Sarajevo on Miljacka Bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, bearing in mind the use of court time, I'm not sure if you are on the right way at the moment. Dealing with the outbreak of the First World War is a very interesting issue, but I think not relevant for the indictment. You should focus on the knowledge of this witness in relation to the allegations against you in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We're discussing the attack against a military convoy, and these are events that were relevant for the break-out of the war in BiH. A military convoy was attacked. There were 23 killed, 47 wounded, and still we haven't seen any proceedings being started -- initiated in relation to this issue, whereas in the previous instance, a whole world war broke out after that. And I'm asking the witness, Shouldn't there have been some trial of these people who killed 23, wounded 47, and captured more than a hundred officers that were officers of a legitimate army of the state? If that was not enough cause for a criminal proceedings to be launched, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the question of, Because of a certain historical event, it was necessary to carry out criminal investigation proceedings, is not part of our trial, especially not the outbreak of the First World War. You should focus on the indictment against you and use this witness. He is very important for you to these topics.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I put this question because I think that the beginning of the war in the Balkans is the beginning of the Third World War. I will try and prove that through witnesses during these proceedings. I will have witnesses who will be able to speak about the start of the war in former Yugoslavia and try to demonstrate whether it was initiated by the peoples of the former Yugoslavia or someone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I repeat, you may call witnesses. That will be proved. But at the moment, you have a witness here who can testify about the relevant events in relation to the indictment against you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could we please have 1D759 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, we see a document here. You're most probably familiar with it. It's a decision by Alija Izetbegovic, dated 27th April 1992, on allowing the army to withdraw from Bosnia. In your response, you told us that MacKenzie and Izetbegovic allowed the army to withdraw, yet four or five days after this decision, you were attacked. Do you remember this decision by Alija Izetbegovic according to which the army was free to withdraw from Bosnia and Herzegovina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen this decision before, but it is dated 27th of April. And, yes, I do know about their position, and I know what requirements this decision brought about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salapura. Please be so kind to look at the first paragraph, the last line: "At the session of the 27th of April, 1992, a decision was reached concerning the withdrawal of units from the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And let me now read to you item 3: "Members of the JNA who, for whichever reasons, do not want to put themselves at the disposal of the state organs of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina are required to leave the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the direction they desire, with the escort of the Ministry of the Interior of the BiH." And then further on: "The dynamics and the axis of their withdrawal will be determined by relevant organs." And so on and so forth. Can you please tell us whether this decision was drafted only for the eyes of the international community, or was it something that should have been in effect, based on the decision reached at the session on the 27th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the reasons were for drafting of this decision, but it was not implemented. I do know that there were some units that started with their withdrawal towards Serbia and were attacked. I know that it was impossible to leave Sarajevo, that the barricades were set up, and ambushes, that any unit attempting to withdraw would have suffered the same consequences as the Command of the 5th Military District. This was, I think, only a farce. I don't know how to call it. Alija was there personally, and still it did not prevent them from attacking us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salapura. Let us now look at decisions of the ministers who were supposed to escort you, according to Alija Izetbegovic, and who, instead, attacked the units of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at document -- thank you, Aleksandar. Document 1D750. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, we can see a document dated 29th of April, which is only two days after Alija's decision concerning so-called peaceful withdrawal of the JNA. This is something drafted by his commander of Territorial Defence, and it is stated: "On the basis of the decision of the president of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," which is the document we've seen before, "concerning the withdrawal of units of JNA, and because this decision was violated, and because the property of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was being stolen, I issue the following order: "Along all the axes of withdrawal of JNA, blocks should be set up. Military facilities should be also encircled and blocked." Under 3: "All unannounced convoys of JNA units, without Ministry of Interior escorts, should be prevented for -- urgently plan and start combat activities in the entire territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And in the framework of the planning, prepare all the measures for protection of population and property." So after this decision that may have been written for the international community and maybe just for the public about peaceful withdrawal of the JNA units, we can see that his minister of defence is issuing an order to block the movement of JNA units, which, in effect, is a declaration of war to JNA. So you, as a soldier, how do you assess this, since you have had intelligence about all such actions by the other party?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already mentioned that all the routes for withdrawal were closed, that any attempt by any unit would end up in them being attacked. You can see this order, and, yes, that's how things were in real life. I can say with absolute certainty that none of the JNA units opened fire first. They were all attacked in their facilities and outside of their facilities, even before this order was issued, even before the order by President Izetbegovic was issued. But that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's see what the minister of interior - 1D753 - wrote in his order, and Alija's order also involved him. So could we please have 1D753 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This seems to be really illegible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We don't have a better version.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note: The text on the screen is illegible, there's no English interpretation, and Mr. Tolimir is probably going to read very fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is an order, and it says: "To Security Services Centres, to all chiefs, public security centres --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, if you want to read it into the record, please do it slowly so that the interpreters can catch it, because there's no interpretation. Slowly, slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What we can see on the screen, the document that we see on the screen, 1D753, is an order by the minister of the interior, Alija Delimustafic, the minister of the interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, who also issued his order on the implementation of the Presidency decision about the withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia, as you can see in the title, and he sent this order to: Security Services Centres; to all chiefs; to all public security stations; and the secretary of the Sarajevo SUP. And now, in the first part or the preamble of the document, it says -- and I'm reading from the third paragraph, where he explains that there was a decision by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina about the withdrawal of the JNA on the 27th of April. And we can see that this an order. Under 1: "Carry out complete blockade of all roads in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on which the units of the former JNA start to withdraw from Bosnia and Herzegovina." Under 2: "Carry out a blockade of the general sector of military facilities." Under 3: "The announced convoys of JNA units, without any police escorts, should be prevented from leaving the barracks." Under 4: "Plan and start combat activities in the entire territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a matter of urgency. Co-ordinate all that with the Territorial Defence of the region." And this is signed by the minister of the interior, Alija Delimustafic. This is the minister of the interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina. My question, Mr. Salapura, is this: Mr. Salapura, bearing in mind that now we have seen two documents -- or, rather, three documents, the first one that was signed by Alija, which formally allowed the JNA to withdraw, the second document, which was issued by the chief of the Territorial Defence, preventing the withdrawal, and the third document, in which the minister of the interior also intends to prevent the withdrawal of the JNA, and both of the last documents order that combat activities should be started as a matter of urgency, would you say that there had been a plan to attack the convoy where you were, as a member of the 2nd Military District in Sarajevo? You were attacked in that convoy. Was that part of a plan? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the attack was carried out in keeping with the orders or directives. I can say also that the evening before the attack happened - I believe that it was one evening before the attack - the minister of the interior was still in our command, and he promised that no attacks would ensue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, what is the date of the document we have in front of us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 27 April, 27 April.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The date is the same as the order issued by Colonel Perica on the 29th of April, 1992, because you can see it here, an order on the implementation of the order of the Presidency of the republic. That decision is referred to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm only asking for the date. No repetition, please. Carry on with your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, could you please admit this document, 1D73 -- 1D753, 1D750, 1D759? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we don't have it on the screen correctly. You should repeat the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, we have just seen 1D753, 1D750, 1D759. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The three documents will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D231, D232 and D233, all marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to be clear, 1D759 will be Exhibit D231, marked for identification. 65 ter 1D750 will be Exhibit D232, also marked for identification. And 65 ter 1D753 will be Exhibit D233. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, all marked for identification, pending translation. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we now see 1D00749. I repeat, 1D00749. And while we are waiting for it to appear, I have to say that this is an overall documentation about the attacks against this column as well as all the other military facilities, even before the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina, or, rather, before the war from Croatia spilled over onto Bosnia-Herzegovina. Let's first look at page 1 in this document, and then I would like to look at page 31, where the attack on the military convoy of the JNA members in Dobrovoljacka Street in Sarajevo, on the 3rd of May, 1992, is described. Thank you. The document was drafted by the Documentation Centre of the Republika Srpska. Thank you. Now we are looking at page 30. I asked for 32. We need 31. Let's look at page 31. Let's look at the introduction. My apologies to the e-court. 31 is the page number. And now we can see where it says: "The attack on the military convoy of JNA members on Dobrovoljacka Street in the 3rd of May, 1992 ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Salapura, is this: Did the attack, indeed, happen on the 3rd of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there's no doubt about that. I didn't remember the date, but you can see here the Documentation Centre has all the relevant materials on which they base this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it was at the beginning of May, so this is the beginning of May. It could have been on the 3rd or on the 4th, but, in any case, it was in the early May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And now we will see this. Paragraph 1: "In a series of attacks on the units of the military formation, which was legal and based on the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the JNA, at the beginning of 1992, we have to look at the activities of the so-called Patriotic League, the Territorial Defence, the Croatian armed forces, on the military convoy of the JNA when the Command of the 2nd Military District in Sarajevo was withdrawing. That happened on the 3rd of May, 1992, around 1700 hours." My question is this: Did the attack, indeed, happen in the afternoon hours, as you can read in the text that I have just read out for you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we go to page 33 in the same document. Thank you. We're looking at page 33. Can we please look at the sixth paragraph. We cannot see it at the moment. Can we scroll up? Yes, very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And the paragraph begins with the following words: "In the course of the attack on the convoy, 23 people were killed, 47 were injured, and about 170 officers, commissioned officers, and soldiers were captured and then escorted to the Partisan facility in Mis Irbina Street and into the Security Services Centre." My question is this: Is the information about the number of dead, injured and captured correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was investigated, and this was proven. The evidence was collected immediately after the event. This is the information compiled by the Documentation Centre, and the information is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you. And can the e-court display page 34 in the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: While this is coming up, I would like to ask the

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Government of the Republika Srpska set it up. Its members are members of the MUP, the military lawyers, and all these people have been dealing with the collection of relevant evidence and documents for a long time; not only about volunteers, but also about crimes and execution sites. Actually, they're dealing with the crimes committed against the Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And when was this centre set up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that that was sometime in 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you saying "1997"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm not sure. I believe so. I know that it was immediately after the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I saw a date of the 3rd of May, 1992, on the heading of this document. Can we go back to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know where that is. This is May 2001, if you're referring to the first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was referring to another page, but that makes it clear. Thank you very much. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes. It's just a clarification. At line 22 -- at page 22, line 1 and 2, you have referred to: "... and I don't think there were any casualties due to," and you've used the word "Zolja fire." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A Zolja is a hand-held reactive grenade-launcher. The calibre is .67 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's look at page 34, please, 34. Thank you. This is 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On page 35, in the second paragraph, there is a reference to the fallen soldiers of the JNA, whose names are listed in here. We will see that later. It also says that: "In the Central Prison and in the cellars of the DTB Partisan facility, and in other Muslim prisons, the following people were killed:" A total of 26 of them who were also killed. So we're talking about a total of 49 who were killed in the convoy that set out from Sarajevo. And on this page, you can also find, in the third paragraph from the bottom, who the suspects for the war crime were, in keeping with Articles 144 and 146 of the Penal Code of the Republika Srpska, and you can see their number and the names: Ejub Ganic, Sefer Halilovic, Alija Delimustafic, whose order we saw, Jusuf Pusic. These are the suspects, those who -- then Selim Hajric and Fikret Becirovic. And here you can also see the names of the eight of them, with the relevant information, their position, and the role they played during the attack against the column. My question is this: Do you know these eight people, especially Avdo Paljeta, who was also a suspect in the commission of the war crime?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean personally?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: No. Do their names ring any bells? Do you know any of them personally? Did you meet any of them personally, like Alija Delimustafic, for example?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've heard of all of them, because they are performing public functions, some are military functions, and so on and so forth. I had two meetings with Delimustafic, personal meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you've heard of all of these people, do you know if any of the persons on this list was processed and were they charged for war crimes, starting with the column in Sarajevo, whereas we saw at the beginning 23 were killed, and then later 26 were killed subsequently?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody ever was brought to trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know that Ejub Ganic was arrested in England, pursuant to a warrant from Serbia, for crimes, but due to pressure and because of other means, he was released and not charged?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I am familiar that that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you are putting lots of questions outside the scope of this case. You should be aware of the time you are using with this witness. This is, in fact, not relevant to the period of time, relevant for the indictment we are dealing with. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we please look at page 35 now so that we can look at the names of officers and soldiers who were killed in the attack on the military column, ranging -- starting from 1 to 33. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question to you is this: Let's not waste time. Do you know anybody from this list? Were they all members of the JNA, consisting of the Command of the 2nd Military District?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know Radulovic, I know Sokic, I know Mihajlovic, Labudovic, Gvozdenovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we also look at the second part of the list on the following page so that the witness could see -- this is page 36, and so that he could see which active-duty military officers were captured. There is a list of that, too. Thank you. Can we also look at page 37, please, and then page 38. Thank you. Can we also look at page 39, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You've just seen the list of captured persons. At the end, I would just like to read the remark: "In this attack, accompanied by proper documentation, i.e., statements of eye-witnesses of the attack, casualties, testimony of those captured, videocassettes, and also reports by commands and documents from archives on accords, and on the basis of medical documentation, as cited, a complete set of information was given, and this represents the ground for criminal charges for suspects suspected of organising, issuing orders, and executing the attack on members of the JNA army in Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please be asked to repeat the second part of his question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You're again making some trouble for the interpreters. Mr. Tolimir, the last part of your question was not interpreted, and the same happened to the answer. The witness was starting very early with his answer. Please repeat the second part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, can we not overlap, please. I asked whether anybody was brought to trial on the basis of this file that is referred to and on the basis of the last sentence that we can see in the last paragraph of this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: So far, nobody has been brought to trial. And this statement by the chief prosecutor of the court in Bosnia-Herzegovina indicates that proceedings are underway.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Salapura. Can we now look at page 7. We're just going to look at the heading and also the location to which it refers. Page 7 is the attack on the municipality of Brod, March/April 1992, and in line 4 it states: "In Sijekovac, in the broader area of the Brcko municipality, on the 26th of March, 1992, there was an attack."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I wanted to know if you know anything about this attack. You were a member of the 2nd Military District at the time, in whose area this was. Can you please tell us anything about that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this attack was carried out even before the armed conflict broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was carried out by members of the HOS of the Croatian Army, from the Croatian part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Sijekovac is a Serbian village close to Brod. It says "Brcko" here, but actually it's not Brcko; it's Brod. The material for this was submitted to The Hague Tribunal here, as far as I know. It's now located at the court in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and these proceedings have not been started.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And on this page, we also see where these numbers begin. This is the last four lines, 1 to 4. We can see the victims are listed here, 1 to 19. We can look at the second page here, number 8, where you can see that the numbers start from 1 and end up at 19. These are the victims. And then on the same page, again starting towards the bottom of the page from 1 to 8, and then from 1 to 65, all information is provided about those suspected of carrying out that attack, and most of them came from Croatia, which is just what you said. And this is inclusive with the number 69 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: -- living in Brod. The resident's address is [indiscernible]. And so on and so forth. Can you please tell us whether Slavonski Brod is in Croatia or Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slavonski Brod is in the Republic of Croatia. It's on the other bank of the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please look at page 13 of this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can also see that an attack on Kupres is referred to here, and it says, under the heading, that this happened on the 3rd of April, 1992, and it says "Donji Malovan," and so on and so forth. Please, can you tell us anything -- or can you tell the Trial Chamber anything about this attack that took place on the 3rd of April, 1992, and was this before the secession and the recognition of the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this took place before. This is also among those initial conflicts, armed conflicts. Those who participated here also belonged to the Croatian paramilitary units and some units of the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, would you please explain the purpose of this line of questions? From page 41 up to page 67, you were dealing with matters that happened -- events that happened in 1992. What is the purpose of these lines of questions and the use of court time?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The purpose is to show how the conflict from Croatia was transferred to Bosnia, and how the conflict was not provoked by the Serbian side, but precisely by the Muslims, who were supported by the international community and recognised as a socialist republic that had seceded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you please explain the relevance for this trial?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The context of the events is this -- actually, the context of that event is something that later had an effect on the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and later it influenced all the activities that I was later involved in, as well as Mr. Salapura, and the activities of the army that we were members of. The event, in a way, was the source of the consequences that we were forced to deal with later. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to have an explanation from a legal point of view. Of course, events in history have a deep influence on actual events. This is normal. We are all part of history. But I would like to have an explanation from a legal point of view. What is the relevance for this trial? You may consult your legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We dispute the adjudicated facts. This is something that you are aware of, as well as the Prosecution, and the completion -- the completeness of the data that is stated there. And we are stating information that is relevant in relation to this witness about the arrival of NATO to our area, and later other areas, under the pretext of peace organisations, and it also has to do with concealing information and not publicly issuing the relevant information. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, does the Prosecution have a position in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would not deign to advise General Tolimir as to how to proceed in the cross-examination of this witness. I think that's within his prerogative. I do share the Court's concerns with respect to the relevance and the propriety of the questions or the line of questions that is being put to this witness. To the extent that General Tolimir disputes the adjudicated facts, it would be helpful to know, in particular, which adjudicated facts he is disputing with respect to the line of questions that he's put to this witness. And I think if he's able to do that, then he can establish at least some relevance -- legal relevance to the case. However, I don't think, to the extent that this was not any substantive part of the witness's direct examination, that it corresponds in any respect to the questions that were put to him and, I think, would exceed the permissible scope of cross-examination, of course, within the discretion of the Court. But I think without any demonstrative relevance to the salient issues with respect to his responsibility for the crimes alleged in the indictment, then I think we're drifting a bit afield of where we should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, are you -- Mr. Tolimir, are you in a position to give us more details about the adjudicated facts you are disputing?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The adjudicated facts refer to the path to independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which specifically actually set off the war. The witness is talking about how the attacks were started by Croats from Bosanski Kupres, that they attacked a legal force that was protecting the Constitution of the SFRY, and we are talking about the particular route to this independence and that the Prosecution adopted as adjudicated facts, facts that were provided to them by Bosnia and Herzegovina. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you give us the numbers of the adjudicated facts?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The first 10, I don't know precisely, but I know that I did read them. And I did tell my legal assistant to dispute them, setting off from this particular aspect or point of view. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First, at page 69, line 20, I think I said "without any demonstrative relevance to the salient issues," so "without" is missing from that sentence. It should read that: "I think without any demonstrative relevance to the salient issues with respect to his responsibility, then we're drifting far afield." With respect to what General Tolimir just represented concerning the adjudicated facts, they are adjudicated facts. This is the point. They have been previously and finally adjudicated in other proceedings and found as such here. They are substantively background evidence relating to the indictment and the conflict which is -- the result of a conflict. I don't see, though, that it is directly related to the evidence that this witness has given in evidence given during his examination-in-chief. I don't see that it is a salient issue that needs to be gone into to the extent that General Tolimir, it appears, intends to go into during the cross-examination of this witness. I don't dispute that to the extent that it rebuts any adjudicated fact or challenges any adjudicated fact, it could be an appropriate avenue for cross-examination, since he's obliged to put questions to a witness that advance his position. I understand that, and we accept that, as the Prosecution. On the other hand, I don't think, to the extent that he's gone into it this far, it is necessary or appropriate with this witness. Perhaps there's another witness that it would be more appropriate to explore these issues with, a historian perhaps, but I don't think it's appropriate, given the nature of this witness's direct testimony, to pursue this avenue on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, during examination-in-chief the witness was asked about his career and about his CV, his places and positions of service in the relevant armies from the beginning of his career; nothing else in relation to this time. Would you like to respond, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. I think that the Defence has the right to dispute, add to, or put the adjudicated facts in a certain context, and this is what I'm doing here. I've taken references from the summary, from the statement that the witness provided to the Prosecution, and we are now on page 6 of the statement. And, secondly, pursuant to your request, I will stop doing that. However, the facts, you can say that Serbia attacked NATO, that Libya attacked NATO, and those statements can be adopted, but this is not interesting. Secondly, during the examination here, all the information that I wrote and that this witness wrote that referred to NATO activities have been placed under the seal of protection. I'm talking about the activities of NATO in Bosnia. I don't know why. Is this a way to protect the concept of the spreading of NATO across protected areas that is now being adopted in Libya and elsewhere? The Ministry of Defence of Serbia, which is an organ authorised by the government to make such a decision, and the Prosecution that disclosed these materials -- have disclosed all the materials which are now in e-court. I am asking Mr. Vanderpuye, is it -- or, rather, I'm asking the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is the Government of Serbia there to protect NATO or its own citizens by presenting them information that I wrote, that this witness wrote, and we sent that information to them for their perusal? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, at the moment we are discussing procedural problems. It's not the moment to put a question to the witness. I would like to know: What are you referring to when you say: "All the information that I wrote and that this witness wrote that referred to NATO activities have been placed under seal of protection"? What do you mean by that? I don't understand that. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'd like to greet everybody. Mr. Tolimir is pointing to the following: You have our list of evidence, which is rather lengthy. It is on 50 or so pages. Most of the documents on the list are under seal, because the institutions of the Government of the Republic of Serbia issued an order, pursuant to Rule 70, that they can be used only in closed sessions, and that is why Mr. Tolimir expresses his positions and views and his very righteous revolt against such practices. And as we're going to see before the course of the trial, there's a lot in the document corroborating the involvement of NATO and some Western countries in the events in Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially when it comes to Srebrenica and the developments that took place, and that we will have an opportunity to discuss during our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, can you please help me? Which documents on this lengthy list are under seal? I don't see any indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I don't know what the case manager has sent. In my file, it says that documents are under seal or at least marked in red. Most of the intelligence reports signed by Mr. Tolimir or Mr. Salapura are, indeed, under seal and can only be used as Rule 70 material, pursuant to the order of the Government of the Republic of Serbia. At least that's what I read on the 65 ter list disclosed to us by the Prosecution. I addressed the Government of the Republic of Serbia at one point in time, asking them to be able to use these documents in open sessions. I received their reply on the eve of the beginning of the trial some year or so ago, in which it says that we could use the document in the same way the Prosecution can use them in closed sessions, without disclosing the documents to the general public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is an important issue. We have to clarify it. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have spoken to Mr. Gajic specifically about this issue. There are a number of documents that we did receive that had Rule 70 restrictions on them. I can't tell you, off the top of my head, specifically which documents they were, but there were quite a number of documents, and we did discuss this issue before. The restriction is that they can be used. However, they have to be used in closed session, and that's basically it. I can get you more specific information about that, and perhaps we can clarify it, but I still think that this is a tangential issue to the nature of the cross-examination, which is where we began. It's a separate question all together than the propriety of the line of questions that's being put to this witness. I see that it's time for the break. It's probably a good opportunity for everybody to take a breather and sit back and assess where we are. And I'll talk to Mr. Gajic during that period of time and see if I can get him appropriate information concerning the restrictions that are in place and the extent of them, and I can inform the Trial Chamber when we return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's a good proposal. Before we break, Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just one thing in order to avoid any confusion. Most of the documents, as you can see, on our exhibit list bears a 65 ter number of the Prosecutor. We'll use them during the cross-examination of this witness. And this is the only thing I wanted to add at the end of this discussion, and what I have in mind is the further course of the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At the outset of this discussion, I was reminding the Defence to make the best use of the court time available. We must have the second break now, and we will resume 20 minutes past 6.00. And the Chamber will consider this situation in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before the break, we dealt with three separate issues. One was the matter of adjudicated facts the accused is challenging, as he told us before the break, and he gave us a reference for approximately the first 10 adjudicated facts. We looked into it, and we see there is one chapter of the decision of the adjudicated facts dealing with 1991 and 1992, the break-up of the former Yugoslavia. These are the Adjudicated Facts 1 through 8. In fact, 8 of the whole of 604 adjudicated facts. Looking into these adjudicated facts, we see nothing which is in any way putting the finger on one warring party. In that case, it is dealing with, in very short terms, with the composition of the Socialist Republic of the former Yugoslavia between 1945 and 1990, and the ethnic composition of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the Communist time, the problems in the late 1980s, and then the declaration of independence by Slovenia and Croatia and the break-off of Macedonia, and then, in relation to our case, number 7, Bosnia began its journey to independence with a parliamentary declaration of sovereignty on the 15th October of 1991. That is, in fact, all. And then you have dealt with it a lot, the recognition of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina by the European Community and by the United States. We don't see that the testimony of this witness is in any way challenging these eight adjudicated facts. This was point 1. The second point - I don't think that there is a need to deal with that and to discuss it at the moment - is the fact that there are restrictions, pursuant to Rule 70, by using certain documents. For sure, we will not do that today, I think. And the third is the use of court time during cross-examination. To make it very clear, Mr. Tolimir, it's up to you to decide which questions you put to a witness, but may I say this: As you are not a lawyer, as you are representing and defending yourself, and because we have a certain responsibility to look at the best use of court time and to make sure that we have not only a fair, but also an expeditious trial, we should assist you and give you some guidance. And we are not cutting questions, but we wanted sometimes to give you a kind of warning. Do the best to use the court time for your defence in the best way. The last hour before we started this discussion, you were dealing with matters which I had to ask you about the relevance and the purpose to put these questions for your purposes. You should continue and bear that in mind. That has something to do with the length of this cross-examination and the hours indicated by you. You can't expect, after this experience, that you will be given many more -- much more time for continuation and concluding your cross-examination. You should continue, and we should use the last half an hour of today's hearing for your cross-examination. Please continue, and bear my words in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for all these admonitions. I was at page 13, as we can see, and I will only speak about the numbers -- well, rather, I will not discuss any other issues. I will just ask the witness whether something is or is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here, we have information about attack against Kupres between 3rd of April and 15th of May, 1992. At the time, did Bosnia secede from Yugoslavia, and was Bosnia recognised by that time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the fighting on Kupres, no, not at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please turn to page 16. I will just put a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were all people captured at Kupres taken to prisons in Croatia; Split, Zadar, Lora and so forth, and were the people who are listed here by name among those missing? For instance, 28 persons were killed, and their remains still haven't been found. We can find that on page 18.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you how many people were killed at Kupres. I do know there was an on-site investigation carried out there by the military police organs of the MUP of Kupres and the corps. I did not have an opportunity to see the report, so I cannot comment on the details therein, because Kupres was at the time in the area of responsibility of the Knin Corps. I was at the time at Manjaca, in the Command of the 2nd Military District, and we did not have all the data -- detailed data available, so I cannot comment this any further or respond to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether on-site investigations were carried out and forensic examination during the autopsy of the bodies that were found in the Kupres area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that they were fully processed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that a criminal report was filed? We can find that on page 24, and there it is mentioned that 74 people were killed. And we can see on page 24 -- can we please have page 24 on the screen. Up until number 73, we will see who were the perpetrators, and in the further text on, 4 to 115, we can see other data. So are you aware that the full criminal report was drafted and that this report was sent to relevant organs?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this was sent to any court or any relevant body.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On page 24, please take a look at numbers 1 to 3. Who were the people who issued orders? Do you know anything about the people listed here, and are these people listed as those who issued orders in the criminal report we are discussing?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only tell you what I see on the screen. I did not know their names. I have heard of Tomislav Filipovic, and only of him. I don't know any of the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at the names listed on pages 24 to page 30. We have 115 people listed as direct perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please turn the page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you have a question for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is my question: Does this criminal report provide precise data about those who issued orders and those who perpetrated the crimes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with the names of the perpetrators. I have heard of Vile [phoen], and there is also mention of a Croatian general, and of several people by the surname of Vile. I have heard that they were involved, but I wasn't following all the events and the criminal reports because this was not part of my jurisdiction. This is something that is the job of MUP and the Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Because all of this was drafted in the Documentation Centre, and because it contains mainly the names of victims, those who issued orders, and direct perpetrators, and it refers to all the events that took place before the break-out of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I will put to you this question: Do you know that any organ of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina acted upon this criminal report? Or to make it more precise, do you know whether any of the organs in Bosnia and Herzegovina has processed the people that are listed in document 1D00749?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for a fact that they were not processed in any way. And what is the status of this case, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, because this is criminal and legal documentation concerning the crimes that happened before the outbreak of war in Bosnia, I would like to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you tell me, how many pages does this document contain?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document has about 135 pages, but about 80 per cent of it is just names of either victims, or perpetrators, or people who were issuing orders. There is only criminal reports and the summary text at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The problem is the amount of work the Translation Unit has to do. We should find a way to reduce this work of translation. We need a translation, of course, but perhaps not the whole document. If it has 130 pages, approximately, we should think about and you should think about only to tender the relevant pages you have used with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I would object, actually, to the admission of this document. I think the witness's testimony is quite clear with respect to his familiarity with its contents, or lack thereof, I should say. He did indicate that he recognised a couple of names that were shown to him, but beyond that, I think he indicated quite clearly that he wasn't familiar with this document, didn't know about the context or what it purports to represent specifically. And I don't think that there's any basis of relevance for the document to be admitted at this stage. If, perhaps, there's another witness that knows more about it, or even if another witness knows more about it, if General Tolimir can establish a nexus between this document and any, as I say, salient issue under the indictment, then I think it might be appropriate, but at this stage I don't think he's established that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the witness indicated several times, like page 78, line 14, line 21; page 79, line 8; that he cannot tell, he cannot comment, and he doesn't know, and it was not his area of responsibility, but of the MUP. You have heard the objection of Mr. Vanderpuye. What is your position.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is my opinion: If this document will not be entered into evidence, then maybe we could have just a number of criminal reports and the number of victims, because there is always an option that we use a different witness for this. When Mr. Rupert Smith was testifying, you suggested that we should ask some other witness, although he was here, but I don't know how to tender a document if one cannot do it through a witness who participated in the events, who was there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I would like to invite you - it is not necessary to do that now - to indicate which pages you have used with the witness, and then we will decide that later. For the moment, we should give it a number and mark it for identification to be able to identify it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D234, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we please have -- or, rather, I'd first like to put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the area of responsibility of your command, was Kupres within that area of responsibility, and was I a member of a unit that was also in the Kupres area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't say it was not part of the area of responsibility. I said that it was in the area of responsibility of the Knina Corps, but that was in the initial stages when the Knin Corps just entered the 2nd Army complement, when they moved to Kozara, and when the communications were not fully functional. What I do know is that the events at Kupres represented one of the first crimes against the Serbian people at the time, and I do know that MUP and the military police were involved in documenting all this. As an intelligence officer, I received whatever information was available, but I did not have all the details, and it was not part of my sphere of activity. I just received some basic information at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salapura. For the sake of the transcript, could you please say: Kupres, as the territory, and the Knin Corps, were they in the area of responsibility of the Command of the 2nd Military District in Sarajevo, where you were serving? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is correct, and that's when it was actually transferred as part of the 2nd. That's the 5th Military District that became the 2nd.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at 65 ter 3527.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, is this a document of the Command of the 2nd Military District of the 16th of May, 1992, which I signed as the chief of the security organ, and was this document sent to the 10th Corps?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was the 10th Corps part of the 2nd Military District?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not disputing that. This just went along the security line, not along the intelligence line, so I didn't receive the information from on-site investigations which were carried out by the MUP units.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So we're talking about the 16th of May. Can we now look at 65 ter 3529, and can I tender this document which talks about the 2nd Military District covering the area of responsibility where the witness was? And the date of the document is the 16th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document 65 ter 3527 will be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D235, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We can see another document here which was created later. The document bears the date the 20th of May, 1992. I also signed this document, and the heading of the document -- actually, the document has the heading "Main Staff of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," to the Intelligence/Security Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is that the transformation you were talking about in your statement, when you talked about the 5th becoming the 2nd Military District? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as I came to Han Pijesak, and I'm unable to tell you the exact date, but this was in May, after the Dobrovoljacka incident, shortly after that, so this Intelligence/Security Administration was formed during that period. There were separate security and intelligence departments, and then the administration was formed separately for intelligence and security affairs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this document as well. Thank you. Could we see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. I would like to see the last page. Thank you. It will be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D236, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we see 1D743 in the e-court now. We'll wait for it to appear on our monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But until we see it, I would just like you, if you remember -- how were these intelligence and security organs created, and then how it came about that the Intelligence and Security Administration was created as one organ? This is on pages 6 and 7 in the Serbian and page 5 in the English.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened following an agreement and conversation between you and me. When I came to Han Pijesak, I was by myself. I didn't have anyone else in this department. There was just me. The same situation was in three other corps. I didn't have enough cadres. Those who were there before they had gone to Serbia, they joined the Army of Yugoslavia, these officers left. I don't need to go into details, but those officers from Serbia who were in that unit had left, gone back, so I was left alone. And that's how we agreed then to form an administration to issue instructions that security officers, since there were more of them, the service was larger in terms of personnel, it was up to strength, so they were given assignments to actually work on intelligence jobs as well, and then that's how we began to create the security organ and the intelligence organs, which then later grew into the Security Administration organ, where you had one chief who was in charge of both lines of activities.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, we mentioned the wrong pages. It's page 9 in English and 10 in Serbian, page 10 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On that page, you speak about this from lines 10 to 32, and we can all see that this is on page 10, where you say exactly what you said now.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And that is how the Administration for Security and Intelligence was created, and we can see that after we had our conversation and agreement, two days after that this was actually implemented. For example, what we see in lines 31 and 32, do you know how the Intelligence and Security Sector was created and what was its role?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, when the sections grew into the administration, as the Army of Republika Srpska began to grow and it began to be staffed, the institutions developed. And along with that, the scale of our assignments grew and expanded. Then it became a sector, because then throughout the whole war, we had a lot of personnel problems, particularly in the intelligence area. We ended the war without an intelligence officer in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, where the security officer was actually carrying out these tasks. We were unable to obtain adequate suitable personnel, and we were unable to train people to be able to carry out those assignments. The sector was the one who co-ordinated both of these organs and regulated the exchange of information, data, and so on and so forth between the two administrations, and that was the link through the sector that led up to the commander, who in that way controlled and commanded both of the organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, practically, what happens with the information that the chief of the sector receives, data of an intelligence nature, and what happens with counter-intelligence information?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Analysis Sector processes the information it receives on a daily basis from the organs that gather such data, they process these intelligence data every day. Then the information is sent to you. You read the information first, and then you would note who the recipients would be, other than the ones that are already mentioned, and to whom specific data should be passed on to; for example, specific intelligence data or counter-intelligence data. You would make a note on the document to whom this data should be handed over, and then you would also issue instructions regarding intelligence data and how the Intelligence Sector would deal with that information; for example, would it be necessary to continue to process or work further on a particular kind of trail or information or should this be handed over to another higher body, who would deal with that information, for example, the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us, briefly, what was the job of the intelligence component in the staff, and what was the job of the security component?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that before. Intelligence Administration exclusively worked on compiling intelligence about the enemy. We already mentioned that. It had to do with the terrain, the timing, the facilities, the plans, the intentions, the forces, and everything that relates to the enemy. Of course, they also dealt with international relations, the international factor, in particular with countries that had a significant effect on the developments in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the political arena, during preparations for peace conferences, talks, because that was also a problem. So these are the spheres of work of the intelligence segment. The Security Service deals with internal matters, with counter-intelligence and security matters within units of the Army of Republika Srpska and on the territory of the AOR, where they co-operate with the MUP, the State Security Service, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at document 203, D203.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: These are the Rules of Service, D203, Rules of Service of Security Organs in the Armed Forces, since in the summary, you did say that for a while you were a security organ.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 9 of these rules, which talks about the tasks and area of activity of the security organs. Thank you. This is page 5 in the Serbian and page 6 in the English. We're reading paragraph 1. Actually, we're looking at Chapter 1, not Chapter 2, so we're looking at Article 1 of Chapter 1. Can we please have that entire paragraph on the screen. Thank you. I quote: "Security organs, as specialist organs of commands, units, institutions and staffs of the armed forces, carry out duties of state security that are placed within their competence by the law and regulations issued pursuant to the law, for the purposes of detecting and preventing activities aimed at subverting or disrupting the social order established by the Constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia ..." End of quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us, briefly, whether these are internal problems that occur within the army in which the security organs are working, and whether they are the ones who are exclusively responsible for internal matters, rather than external and intelligence matters? This is what it states here, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is their main area of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If, by their methods --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, it is 7.00. We have to adjourn for the day. We will resume tomorrow at 9.00 in Courtroom III, so that we have the opportunity to sit in all three courtrooms this week. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 5th day of May, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.
